Summary of the article:
This paper presents an Open Science Protocol specifically tailored for the Integrated
Assessment Modeling (IAM)community, based on a survey of IAM teams. The protocol is
designed to improve the transparency, accessibility, and reusability of IAM models and outputs
by aligning with the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and TRUST
(Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, Technology) principles. The study
highlights current challenges in implementing open science within IAMs—such as inconsistent
documentation, limited vetting of outputs, and barriers to sharing data—and offers practical
guidance to overcome these. By fostering better communication and usability of models,
especially for policymakers, the protocol aims to enhance the credibility and impact of IAMbased climate assessments.

Summary of the article:
This paper presents an Open Science Protocol specifically tailored for the Integrated
Assessment Modeling (IAM)community, based on a survey of IAM teams. The protocol is
designed to improve the transparency, accessibility, and reusability of IAM models and outputs
by aligning with the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and TRUST
(Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, Technology) principles. The study
highlights current challenges in implementing open science within IAMs—such as inconsistent
documentation, limited vetting of outputs, and barriers to sharing data—and offers practical
guidance to overcome these. By fostering better communication and usability of models,
especially for policymakers, the protocol aims to enhance the credibility and impact of IAMbased climate assessments.
Details related to the questions above (where I answered partly):
The paper acknowledges the importance of the FAIR (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and
Reusability) and TRUST (Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology)
principles but does not fully explore their practical implementation within Integrated Assessment
Models (IAMs). A deeper engagement with recent literature and case studies specific to IAMs and
these principles would strengthen both the theoretical foundation and practical relevance.
While the survey design is appropriate for gathering qualitative insights, the methodology section
lacks sufficient detail. Key elements such as the full survey instrument, sample size, and selection
process are missing, which limits transparency and hampers replicability. Providing this
information, along with a clearer description of how responses were analyzed, would enhance the
robustness of the conclusions.
The protocol presented is promising, with clearly outlined steps. However, it would benefit from
further elaboration, particularly regarding practical challenges encountered, strategies for
adaptation across IAM contexts, and concrete examples of successful implementation. Additional
data—such as more detailed documentation, case studies, or checklists—would improve the
transparency and reusability of the work.




Although the interpretation of survey results is reasonable, it relies heavily on qualitative insights.
Incorporating statistical analysis or quantitative data could provide stronger support for the
findings. The conclusions align with the presented results but could be made more compelling
through the inclusion of real-world applications that demonstrate the protocol’s effectiveness and
impact.

use the R code and with which data.
- The data is deposited in Zenodo as xlsx file which is not an open format. csv file (text file) would
be better for reuse.
- Figure 1 is unreadable on my laptop (too small).
- The survey results file (available at [external resource identifier omitted] contains 9 entries,
suggesting that fewer than 10 individuals responded to the survey.
Recommendation:
There are a few areas where additional details and refinement could help to strengthen the
scientific rigor of your paper. Below are some specific suggestions:
1. Strengthen the Theoretical Framework
It would be beneficial to gain a deeper understanding of how the FAIR and TRUST principles can
be practically applied to IAMs (in detail because in the paper, the 15 FAIR principles are not
addressed with sufficient details). This will help better align the theoretical foundation of your
protocol with current best practices in Open Science and ensure its relevance to the IAM
community.
2. Enhance Methodological Transparency
The methodology section could be improved by providing more detailed information about the
survey design. For instance, explain why the sample size and the selection process of survey
participants were sufficient for this work.
3. Improve the GitHub Repository
The GitHub repository could be enhanced by providing clear documentation on how to use the
R code and apply it to the provided data. Additionally, I suggest switching the data format from
XLSX to an open format like CSV to facilitate easier reuse and interoperability with other tools.
4. Enhance Visual Accessibility
Figure 1 is not easily readable on standard devices. I recommend increasing the resolution and
size of the figures to improve accessibility, ensuring that they are clearly visible to a broader
audience.
5. Increase Survey Sample Size
Given that the survey currently includes fewer than 10 responses, I suggest reaching out to more
IAM teams to increase the sample size. A larger sample would improve the representativeness
of the findings. It would also be helpful to acknowledge the potential limitations posed by the
small sample size and how these might affect the interpretation of your results.

Using survey data, this manuscript investigates open science practices (including barriers and
challenges) in integrated assessment modeling (IAM) teams. Furthermore, this manuscript
proposes an open science protocol to address some key challenges and barriers (such as data
weight, lack of time, awareness or knowledge, etc.) in the use of open science within integrated

The authors provide sufficient context and information (e.g. packages, checklist, softwares,

I do believe that this manuscript would make a great addition to the body of literature on open

benefits of OS) which could cover some recent empirical research results/literature on these
topics.
Further, while I also greatly appreciate the transparency and the sharing of the data, codes,
protocols, etc., I think the manuscript would also benefit to have a dedicated methodology
section; most of the information is already available in the “Survey Results” section. I would just
separate it into two sections and flesh it out a little bit more if/when needed with some descriptive
information about the methods, participants, etc.

Introduction/review of literature:
Regarding OS initiatives in the second paragraph: I would clarify a couple of things
regarding the US’ policies. Many US OS policies (including the NIH’s) are normally called

Nelson Memo (Refer 1) has also sparked a new generation of OS policies in the US; the NIH’s
latest policy was recently released. In short, I would cover the Nelson Memo and then would
give some of the newest policies as examples instead of the NIH’s previous 2021 policy.
In the third paragraph (resources) I would also mention an OA repository, given how
important they have been. OpenAIRE/CERN’s Zenodo or PubMed Central would be a good
example.

section examined the management of project outcomes, addressing output
standardization, the vetting process, output storage, and results presentation. Finally, the

This survey was sent to all modeling teams from the IAM COMPACT 46 and DIAMOND 56
consortia, gathering a total of 13 responses. IAM COMPACT, a Horizon Europe research
project, aims to support the assessment of global climate goals and the design of the next
round of Nationally Determined Contributions and policy planning beyond 2030. At its core
